opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest gains will come from agents rather than chat. In 2024 and 2025 the focus was on making models smarter at answering questions: better reasoning, better benchmarks. In 2026 I think the real productivity jump comes from models that can actually do work over long horizons. They take a task, break it down, use tools, write and run code, check their own results, and keep going for hours rather than seconds.

Coding is the clearest example, and it's already happening. You can see the shift from autocomplete, to writing a function, to now handing off a whole feature or a whole bug-fixing session. Code is the natural first domain because the environment gives you verifiable feedback: the tests pass or they don't. That makes it a good fit for reinforcement learning, and I expect that pattern to spread to other kinds of knowledge work where you can build a good environment and a good reward signal.

So for me, three things drive it. The first is RL scaling on real-world, agentic tasks, not just math puzzles. The second is longer context and better memory, so the model can keep track of a complex job without losing the thread. The third, which people underestimate, is efficiency. If inference stays expensive and slow, you can't let an agent think and act for hours. Cost and speed will decide whether these capabilities reach ordinary people's daily work.

The bottleneck is shifting from "Is the model smart enough?" to "Can we build the right environments, feedback, and infrastructure so the model can work reliably on its own?" Whoever solves that will see the biggest productivity gains.

r003.rationale: It discusses agents, but does not say that collaboration among multiple agents reduces task-completion time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that the biggest gains in 2026 won't come from a single dramatic breakthrough in base model capability. They'll come from models finally becoming reliable enough to be trusted with long, multi-step work, and from the infrastructure around them catching up.

Let me break that into three pieces.

First, agentic reliability. For the past couple of years we've had models that are impressive on a single turn but fragile over twenty or fifty steps. The error compounds. What changed over the last year, and what I think accelerates in 2026, is reinforcement learning on real task environments rather than on static preference data. When you train a model on whether it actually finished the job, with verifiable outcomes like tests passing or a document meeting a spec, you get a very different kind of robustness. Coding is the first domain where this is obvious, because the reward is so clean. But the same recipe is spreading to data analysis, research synthesis, and operational work.

Second, context and memory. A lot of what looks like a capability gap is actually a context gap. The model doesn't know your codebase, your team's conventions, what you decided last month. In 2026 I expect the practical frontier to be less about raw reasoning and more about systems that persist knowledge across sessions, retrieve the right things at the right time, and know when they don't know. That's unglamorous engineering, but it's where hours of human time get saved.

Third, cost. The reasoning-heavy models from 2024 and 2025 were expensive to run at scale. Distillation, better sparse architectures, and smarter allocation of test-time compute are bringing the cost of good reasoning down fast. When it's cheap to run a capable model continuously in the background rather than calling it occasionally, the economics of what counts as automatable shift a lot.

If I had to summarize, I'd say 2026 is the year AI stops being a tool you consult and starts being a colleague you delegate to. Not for everything, and with real supervision. But the shift from assistant to agent is the productivity story, and in my view it's mostly a story about training on real tasks and building the scaffolding around the model rather than about bigger pretraining runs alone.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest gains will come from AI being able to complete a whole task, rather than just help with one step. Writing code is one step. Understanding the requirement, making the change, testing it, and checking whether it actually solves the problem—that’s where the productivity gain becomes much more meaningful.

For that to work, we need progress in reliability, in how models use tools, and in how they maintain context over longer tasks. A system can look very impressive in a short demonstration, but if you have to intervene constantly, it’s hard to delegate real work to it.

I’d also pay attention to inference cost. When useful intelligence becomes cheaper, you can afford to have models check their work, explore alternatives, and support many more everyday workflows.

So my expectation for 2026 is that the important change will be in how much work we can confidently hand over. And that will depend on the surrounding software and how people organize their work, as well as on the models themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest gains will come from AI moving beyond answering questions to completing useful pieces of work. Writing a draft is helpful, but taking a task through research, execution, checking, and revision could have a much larger impact.

For that to work, models need to become more reliable, use tools well, and understand the context of the work. A system that gives an impressive answer once is different from one you can depend on every day. The cost of checking and correcting its output matters as much as how quickly it generates something.

So I would watch areas where results can be tested clearly, such as coding, and where people repeat similar workflows. My expectation is that productivity gains will come from a combination of better models and better integration into those workflows. The key question is how much useful work people can finish with AI, including the time they spend supervising it.
